name: Jalanatheswarar Temple, Thakkolam
deity: Shiva as Jalanatheswarar, lord of the waters, in a lingam of sand, with the Goddess Giriraja Kannikambal
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the Thiruooral of the Tevaram, sung by Sambandar (7th century); Pallava foundation with Chola inscriptions
summary: Near Arakkonam, where Nandi is said to pour the Ganga from his mouth, Shiva as Jalanatheswarar dwells in a lingam of sand that no hand may touch — the Thiruooral that Sambandar sang.

sections.history: Thakkolam is a village of Ranipet district near Arakkonam, by the Kosasthalaiyar river. Its temple to Shiva as Jalanatheswarar, called Thiruooral in the hymns, is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Sambandar. The shrine is of Pallava foundation, and its walls are crowded with Chola records — from Aditya I, from Parantaka I across nearly thirty years of his reign, and from Rajendra I, Kulottunga III and Rajaraja III — some naming the settlement Aparajita-chaturvedimangalam. The village's name is also written into history by the battle of Takkolam, fought nearby around 949 between the Cholas and the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III, in which the Chola prince Rajaditya fell.
sections.architecture: The temple's heart is unusual: the lingam of Jalanatheswarar is formed of sand, an earth lingam honoured as Theenda Thirumeni, the sacred form that is not touched by hand. The Goddess Giriraja Kannikambal, daughter of the mountain king, has her own shrine. Within the walls are a hall for Nataraja, a shrine of Dakshinamurthy and a shrine of Gangadhara, west of which lies the Sathya Ganga theertham, the spring at the centre of the temple's story. The style of its older sculpture points to Pallava patronage.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that the sage Uthathi guided Nandi to bring the waters of the Ganga here, and that Nandi poured them through his mouth — the source of the Sathya Ganga theertham, from whose Nandi water is said to flow when the river runs high. The sand lingam carries its own story: in a flood the Goddess is said to have clasped it to her and saved it, leaving her imprint on it, which is why it is never touched. Another tradition places Daksha's sacrifice here, broken up by Veerabhadra, and hears in the village's name the cry Daksha raised as he fell.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva year: Pradosham evenings, Maha Shivaratri, Karthigai Deepam and Arudra Darshan before Nataraja are the customary observances, and the days sacred to Sambandar recall his visit. Confirm festival dates locally.
sections.experience: Thakkolam is a place for the attentive pilgrim: worship before the sand lingam that may not be touched, a pause at the theertham the legend says Nandi brought, and time with the old sculpture and the long Chola inscriptions on the walls, a record of centuries of devotion. The Tevaram shrine of Thiruvalangadu lies within easy reach.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thakkolam lies about 12 km south-east of Arakkonam and is reached by road from Arakkonam, which is a major railway junction on the Chennai suburban and long-distance lines. Kanchipuram is about 25 km to the south, and Chennai International Airport is the nearest airport.
